content: Bacterial meningitis is a serious condition that continues to cause significant illness and death among neonates and children, particularly in developing countries. Even when children survive, they may suffer from long-term neurological complications, such as hearing loss, developmental delays, and cognitive impairments. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of using corticosteroids as an additional treatment to reduce mortality and neurological complications in neonates with bacterial meningitis. To gather evidence, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE via PubMed, African Index Medicus, CINAHL, EMBASE, and the metaRegister of Controlled Trials. The search included studies published up to July 2015. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs that investigated the use of adjunctive corticosteroids in neonates with bacterial meningitis. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for eligibility and extracted data on study methods, participant characteristics, interventions, and outcomes. The primary outcomes of interest were all-cause mortality until hospital discharge, sensorineural hearing loss at one year, neurological deficits or developmental delays at two years, and adverse events. Statistical measures such as risk ratio (RR), risk difference (RD), and the number needed to treat for an additional beneficial or harmful outcome (NNTB or NNTH) were calculated when applicable. The quality of evidence was assessed using the Cochrane risk of bias tool and the GRADE system. The review identified two trials involving a total of 132 participants that met the inclusion criteria. One of these trials was a quasi-randomized study. The use of adjunctive corticosteroids was associated with a reduction in the risk of death (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.88; RD -0.19, 95% CI -0.33 to -0.04; NNTB = 6). However, the evidence supporting this finding was of very low quality. Corticosteroids did not significantly reduce the incidence of sensorineural hearing loss at two years (RR 1.80, 95% CI 0.18 to 18.21; RD 0.04, 95% CI -0.12 to 0.21), based on one study with 38 participants and low-quality evidence. In one trial, dexamethasone was found to reduce the likelihood of hearing loss at four to ten weeks post-discharge (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.98; RD -0.25, 95% CI -0.48 to -0.01), but this evidence was also of low quality. Data on other outcomes of interest were insufficient. In conclusion, the available evidence from two small trials of very low quality suggests that adjunctive corticosteroids may reduce mortality and, to a lesser extent, hearing loss in neonates with bacterial meningitis when used alongside standard antibiotic therapy. However, there is no clear evidence of benefit in reducing long-term neurological complications. To confirm these findings, future research should focus on conducting well-designed trials with larger sample sizes, evaluating a broader range of clinically relevant outcomes, and ensuring adequate follow-up.
